Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Public Defender
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Overeating: I eat more than usual to distract myself or feel better, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Vignette:
The rain had turned the pavement outside the municipal bus terminal into a slick mirror when Minh finally saw his younger brother on the ground. He had only turned away to purchase a carton of milk, and when he looked back, a figure in a heavy coat was already moving toward him, then past him, before the heavy thud of a body striking concrete finally cut through the street noise. Minh’s mind never assembled the sequence into a continuous narrative. What remained were disconnected snapshots: the glint of a silver zipper, the way his brother’s hand had fallen open on the wet tiles, a sharp, wet gasp that seemed to hang in the air long after the footsteps faded. For months, that gasp returned unbidden, replaying in his head whenever the silence grew too heavy, each recurrence dragging the same hollow, suffocating dread to his throat. Soon after the funeral, Minh found himself standing at the front door long after nightfall, his key turning in the deadbolt not once, but four or five times, each click met with a sharp pull of the handle to verify. He did this for the windows, too, pressing his forehead against the cool glass to scan the empty street before forcing himself to the bedroom. When a car backfired two blocks away or a neighbor’s screen door slammed, his body would lock, his shoulders hiking to his ears as if bracing for impact, even though nothing was wrong. Alongside these physical reactions, he experienced sudden, unbidden waves of fear, anger, and shame. He was certain he should have done more, that his own survival felt like a quiet betrayal of the man who never made it home. The years that followed slowly hardened into routine. Minh returned to the county courthouse, but the familiar corridors now felt suffocating. He caught himself assessing every person who entered his office, his gaze fixed on their hands, their posture, the set of their jaw, searching for the quiet tell of a dangerous man. When a client’s file detailed an assault, he would close the folder and turn to the refrigerator, pulling out containers he did not need. He ate past fullness. The repetitive motion of chewing sat heavily in his chest, a separate rhythm that competed with the quiet of the empty house. Over weeks, he stopped watching the evening news, avoided true-crime podcasts, and deliberately looked away from newspaper headlines about violent crime, telling his paralegals that he was simply swamped with discovery. Over months, the avoidance bled into his practice; he began declining the monthly firm dinners, claiming exhaustion, and found himself struggling to sit through depositions because the opposing counsel’s rapid movements made his chest tighten with a dread he could not name. His wife had passed three years prior, leaving him to navigate the quiet house alone, and the grief that surfaced during the fragmented recall of that terminal afternoon had grown too loud to ignore. At sixty-eight, the weight of keeping his world tightly controlled had begun to fray his hands. He had come to believe that if he stopped monitoring the locks or scanning the room, the past would simply step through the door. It was his daughter who finally insisted he call, pointing out that he could no longer read a legal brief without his vision blurring, that his children were walking on eggshells around a man who flinched at the sound of a coffee cup setting down on a saucer. Minh sat in the clinician’s office now, his hands clasped tightly over his knees, terrified that speaking about the past would make the memory real again, yet desperate for a way to finally let his guard down without feeling the ground give way.
